content: The role described was that of a male servant who, among other responsibilities, was tasked with cleaning the monarch’s posterior after a bowel movement. During the early years of King Henry VIII’s reign, this position was granted to the king’s favored companions, often young noblemen or sons of prominent gentry who spent time with him in the Privy Chamber. Over time, these individuals evolved into de facto personal secretaries for the king, performing a range of administrative duties within his private quarters. This position was highly coveted, as it provided unparalleled access to the king’s attention and favor. It is evident that serving the royal body in this capacity was regarded as entirely honorable, devoid of any sense of degradation or humiliation. The mere word of a Gentleman of the Privy Chamber was considered sufficient evidence of the king’s will, and the Groom of the Stool carried with him the ineffable charisma associated with the monarchy. One notable individual who held this position was Sir Henry Norris, who served as Groom of the Stool under Henry VIII. He was later executed for allegedly engaging in an affair with Anne Boleyn. A similar role, known as the Porte-coton, existed in the French royal court. The position of Groom of the Stool, in a less scatological form, persisted until 1901.
